blocks.text: A program can compile, print the expected answer, and still leave its next caller with a dangling reference. A resource wrapper can release memory correctly while a failed update publishes half of a new dataset. A view can make a transformation elegant while hiding that its input has already disappeared. Modern C++ is not a collection of newer syntax that makes these problems vanish. It is a way to make ownership, values, constraints, and state transitions explicit enough to reason about them.

blocks.text: This volume continues the language foundation established in Book I. Its goal is to help you design ordinary C++ code whose behavior remains understandable when values are copied, resources move, containers change, parsing fails, and external operations stop halfway through. It preserves the complete twenty-one-chapter curriculum, including every numbered section and subsection. The expansion adds sustained explanation, failure analysis, guided practice, executable supplemental labs, and a stronger application acceptance exercise.

topics.title: Audience and progression
topics.summary: Begin after you can write functions, use basic containers, understand references and pointers, define simple classes, and compile a multi-file application. Book I supplies that foundation. This volume revisits lifetime and class invariants when modern features make those ideas more demanding; it does not assume that a short introduction to pointers already resolves every ownership question.

blocks.text: Chapters 1–6 establish values, invariants, RAII, copying, moving, and smart ownership. Chapters 7–10 develop meaningful operators, inheritance, runtime polymorphism, and composition. Chapters 11–18 cover templates, concepts, lambdas, iterators, containers, algorithms, and ranges. Chapters 19–21 integrate richer result types, external resources, and a complete reporting application. The appendices provide complete supplemental programs and a reusable review method.

blocks.text: The book intentionally stops short of teaching concurrency, lock-free algorithms, operating-system networking, GPU programming, or hard-real-time guarantees. Those subjects belong to later volumes. A shared pointer is discussed as a lifetime mechanism, not as proof that shared data is thread-safe. A steady clock is discussed as a timing vocabulary, not as proof that a program meets a deadline. Keeping those boundaries visible is part of professional competence.

blocks.text: The reference directory retains links to the C++20 working draft N4861 and relevant original project documentation. It also identifies living primary documents used for editorial cross-checks. A living draft can contain features or wording newer than C++20; it is not silently treated as the deployed language baseline. The examples avoid relying on later conveniences such as C++23 range-to-container helpers or optional monadic operations.

blocks.text: Standards describe required behavior; compiler and library implementations determine which facilities are available in your installed environment. Use the exact compiler, standard-library version, flags, and source when reproducing an issue. A different front end using the same standard library is useful additional evidence, but it is not an independent test of every library implementation. The verification report states this distinction.

topics.title: Read for a decision, then trace the mechanism
topics.summary: Before studying a feature, identify the question it should answer. Does a caller need a value or a borrow? Does a failed operation preserve accepted state or only prevent a leak? Is a view a retained recipe or a completed snapshot? Is a search result a boundary or a match? These distinctions are more useful than memorizing a list of type names.

blocks.text: A failed negative-input application run can be the expected outcome of a passing fixture. Read the fixture’s specified exit status and diagnostic before treating every nonzero process exit as a broken test. Conversely, a successful process exit is not enough when its output or retained state violates the contract. The runner checks the stated behavior, not just whether a process started.

topics.title: Source, output, and exercise conventions
topics.summary: Every complete code listing is inserted from a real source file at assembly time. The editable chapter files contain include markers; the finished manuscript and books contain the expanded listings. This prevents a separately edited listing from quietly drifting away from the delivered program. Smaller inline fragments illustrate a local expression and are not necessarily standalone programs.

topics.title: Use failure deliberately and safely
topics.summary: Supplemental experiments inject failures through controlled test types and stream buffers. They do not rely on exhausting the host’s memory, corrupting the filesystem, or executing known undefined behavior. A distinct simulated-failure type prevents an expected-exception catch from swallowing an assertion failure. The tests verify the precise state boundary promised by the operation.

Windows and macOS execution, independent standard-library implementations, hostile-input security assessment, and official EPUBCheck conformance are not implied by the local checks. Consult the actual report rather than inferring broader validation from a successful build.
